newsitem.title: USA: U.S MUNICIPALS - up, but not enough for refundings.
newsitem.headline: U.S MUNICIPALS - up, but not enough for refundings.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds rose strongly on Thursday, reassured by data that showed inflation was moderate, but the market has not erased enough of its recent, big losses to attact refundings in any volume.
"High-grades are up an 02 overall. It's up an 03 on the longer-end," said a municipal analyst who spoke on condition of anonymity. He added dollar bonds climbed 1/4 of a point to 3/8ths.
Before the market's big nosedive since late July, when yields on the benchmark, 30-year Treasury bond were as low as around 6.30 percent, a number of issuers were considering refundings.
However, several of these offerings went back on the day-to-day calender when the fixed-income yields climbed sharply due to fears that the economy was growing more swiftly than expected.

While the yield on the 30-year Teasury bonds has fallen sharply from as high as 6.67 percent on August 12, a trader noted that the market has a ways to go before potential refundings, which were on the fence a few weeks ago, become attractive.
"I think we have to get back at least to the highs and maintain them," he said. The 30-year Treasury bond yielded 6.56 percent in late trade on Thursday.

Houston, which was considering an approximately $400 million sale of water and sewer refunding bonds, said the deal, which was planned when the bond yields were at their lows, now was up in the air. There had been speculation that the deal would be priced during the week of August 18.
However, at least a few issuers plan to go ahead with refundings. For example, Kent County, Michigan, on August 21 expects to competitively sell nearly $83 million of refunding bonds.

Next week's new issue calender was projected at about $1.8 billion, which would make it one of the five smallest weeks seen this year, according to preliminary estimates from the Reuters Municipal Bond Information Group.

A total of about $683 million of competitive sales were on the calender. After Kent County, the next biggest offering was a $68 million sale by the Louisville, Kentucky, Metropolitan Sewer District, also planned for August 21.
The negotiated calender preliminarily was forecast at $1.1 billion, and that list was led by a $200 million sale of revenue bonds by St Louis through Bear Stearns.

Treasury bonds added to strong gains seen on Wednesday, after consumer spending, which accounts for two-thirds of the U.S. economy, on Wednesday was reported to have climbed 0.6 percent, just a bit less than forecast.
On Thursday, bond prices rallied again as the market reacted to a moderate 0.2 percent rise in the Consumer Price Index for July, which matched forecasts.

And a modest, 0.2 percent gain in industrial production reported by the Federal Reserve also mirrored forecasts, and was at least partly countered by a drop in capacity utilization to 83.1 percent from a downwardly revised reading of 83.3 percent in June.
In the secondary market, E-470 Public Highway Authority, Colorado, Revenues of 2026, which pay a five percent coupon, were offered at 5.46 percent, NET, down two basis points.
And Massachusetts Bay Transportation Bay Transportation Authority bonds of 2024, which also carry a five percent coupon, were bid at 5.53 percent, NET, down six basis points.
In Chicago futures markets, the September municipal bond futures closed up 23 ticks at 119-25/32. The climb was mirrored by Treasury bonds, which rose 25 ticks to 113-20/32.
The MOB spread stood at plus 197 ticks, two ticks below Wednesday's close.
